# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

## No skin-tone or race label {#sec-limitation-skin-tone}

CelebA labels neither skin tone nor race, so the bias breakdown cannot say whom the recognition models fail by either. That is the largest gap in it: differences by race and country of birth are among those NIST's demographic tests of face recognition report, and they are the ones this breakdown cannot see. CelebA's Pale_Skin label is no substitute (#10). It is an annotator's judgement of how pale the skin looks in one photo, not a measure of skin tone, it marks too few gallery-eligible identities to form a group, and its complement, not pale, would lump every other skin tone together. Measuring them would take a benchmark labelled for skin tone, which Ryuk does not use; @sec-data-limitations states the gap for the data.

## Annotator labels, not identity {#sec-limitation-labels}

```{python}
#| label: limitations-setup
from pathlib import Path

from ryuk.evaluation.names import model_name
from ryuk.evaluation.results import read_results
from ryuk.evaluation.tables import bias_breakdown

# Quarto runs the kernel in report/, so the committed results are one level up.
limits = read_results(Path("../evaluation/results.json"))
assert limits is not None and limits.learning is not None and limits.bias is not None
assert limits.identification is not None
limits_gallery = len(limits.identification.selection("test").gallery)
knn = [(c.model, c.method("knn").hyperparameter) for c in limits.learning.models]
assert all(chosen is not None for _, chosen in knn)
# Every model searches the same grid.
knn_grids = {tuple(chosen.candidates) for _, chosen in knn}
assert len(knn_grids) == 1
knn_candidates = list(knn_grids.pop())
knn_edge = [model_name(m) for m, chosen in knn if chosen.value == max(knn_candidates)]
assert len(knn_edge) == 2
# The smallest group with an estimated FPIR, for the first active model under its live rule.
limits_breakdown = bias_breakdown(limits)
limits_groups = [g for a in limits_breakdown.attributes for g in a.groups if g.fpir is not None]
smallest = min(limits_groups, key=lambda g: g.non_mated_probes)
```

The bias breakdown's Male and Young are CelebA's labels: binary judgements by its annotators of how each celebrity looked in each photo, turned into one label per identity by majority. They are not anyone's self-identified sex or gender, nor a measured age; they cannot represent people outside the binary, and "not young" is not an age band. A disparity by these labels is a disparity by how annotators saw the faces, which may differ from how the people identify.

## The edge of the kNN grid {#sec-limitation-knn-grid}

kNN chose k = `{python} f"{max(knn_candidates):g}"`, the largest value on its grid of `{python} ", ".join(f"{v:g}" for v in knn_candidates)`, for `{python} " and ".join(knn_edge)`. A larger k might have scored better on the validation draw, and the finding that kNN falls short of best photo holds only for this grid. The grid was fixed before the test draw was scored and was deliberately not widened after the test results were seen: widening it then would have made the test draw a second validation draw.

## Wide intervals for small groups {#sec-limitation-small-groups}

Groups with at least `{python} limits.bias.min_identities` identities are estimated, but many are small enough that their intervals are wide and a real disparity could go unseen. The photo conditions rest on a few hundred probes each; the smallest group with an FPIR for `{python} model_name(limits_breakdown.model)` is "`{python} smallest.label`", with `{python} smallest.non_mated_probes` non-mated probes, and its FPIR interval spans `{python} f"{100 * smallest.fpir.ci.low:.2f}"`% to `{python} f"{100 * smallest.fpir.ci.high:.2f}"`%. The worst-to-best FPIR ratio is a ratio of two point estimates, the lower often resting on a handful of false alarms, and carries no interval of its own.

## The learned rule and gallery size {#sec-limitation-gallery-size}

The learned decision rule was fitted and frozen on galleries of `{python} limits_gallery` identities, and its second input, the gap to the runner-up, depends on how many others could be the runner-up. A live watchlist is usually far smaller, and with one person on it the live monitor takes the gap as 0. The rule does not run live for any model, so nothing depends on it today, but its measured performance says nothing about how it would behave at the watchlist's own size.

## Random impostors {#sec-limitation-impostors}

Each same-person threshold is frozen, and its false-accept rate measured, on impostor pairs of random CelebA identities (@sec-eval-live-same-person). A photo an operator adds to the wrong person of interest is unlikely to be of a random stranger: it is more likely of someone who looks like them, and a look-alike scores closer to the person than a stranger does, so more such photos would pass unwarned than the measured rate says. The rate is a floor for those mistakes, not an estimate of them. CelebA also files a few people under two identities, whose pairs count as impostors though they show one person, which pushes the measured rate up slightly.

## Possible training-set overlap {#sec-limitation-overlap}

LFW and CelebA are photos of celebrities gathered from the web, and the recognition models were trained on large face datasets gathered the same way: ArcFace's weights on WebFace600K, FaceNet's on VGGFace2. Some of the benchmarks' celebrities may therefore be in the models' training sets. If they are, the models have learnt to tell those people apart before, which would flatter both the LFW accuracies and the CelebA rates. The published LFW figures carry the same caveat, so the comparison with them is like for like, but the CelebA rates may overstate how a model will do on faces it has never seen, such as those of the persons of interest an operator enrols. How much they would is not measured here: it would need each training set's identity list, matched against the benchmarks'. @sec-data-limitations states it for the data.

## No liveness check {#sec-limitation-liveness}

Ryuk has no liveness or anti-spoofing check. Nothing in the pipeline tells a live face from a printed photo or a phone screen held up to the webcam, so such a picture is detected, scored and matched like a face, and can open a sighting. A match therefore says that a face resembling the person of interest was in front of the camera, not that the person was. Presentation attacks were out of scope and nothing about them was measured.

## The unmeasured confirmation rule {#sec-limitation-confirmation}

The confirmation rule of @sec-innovation-confirmation, which opens a sighting once a person of interest is matched in at least half the frames over a short window, is a design choice, not a measurement. Measuring it would need labelled video: footage of people on and off a watchlist, with the frames each is present in marked, from which to count how often a sighting opens for the wrong person, opens late or not at all, or splits one presence into two. None was available, and CelebA's still photos cannot stand in for it. The per-frame rates of @sec-evaluation bound only part of the picture. If frames erred independently, requiring several matches would make a false sighting far rarer than a false match in one frame; but consecutive frames of one face are nearly alike, as one identity's probes are, so a face that is falsely matched once is likely to be matched again, and the rule's real false-sighting rate is unknown.

## What purge cannot erase {#sec-limitation-purge}

Purge erases a person of interest from Ryuk's database: their rows go in one transaction, SQLite's `secure_delete` overwrites what they held with zeros, and the rollback journal is truncated at commit, so neither file keeps their faces. It cannot reach what lies beneath the file. An APFS snapshot is a read-only copy of a whole volume. Time Machine, when it is on, takes one of a Mac's startup disk about every hour and keeps it for 24 hours, keeps the one of its last successful backup until the space is needed, and takes another before each macOS update, besides its backups; a btrfs snapshot keeps a point-in-time copy of one subvolume. A snapshot taken while a person was enrolled keeps their faces until it is deleted. A filesystem that writes changed data to new blocks, as btrfs does by default, puts the zeros in new blocks and leaves the faces in the old ones. The journal, which held a copy of every page the purge zeroed, frees its blocks at commit without overwriting them, and an uploaded photo over 1 MB passes through a temporary file whose blocks are freed, not overwritten. An SSD, which every current Mac has, may also keep old bytes in flash its controller has not yet erased, even under zeros written in place. Moving the database would not help on a Mac, whose local snapshots cover the whole startup disk, and vacuuming it after a purge would add nothing to `secure_delete`. A face purged from Ryuk is gone from the application and its files, not necessarily from the disk.

## No authentication {#sec-limitation-auth}

The service has no login and no audit trail. It serves one operator on the machine it runs on: it binds to loopback and refuses requests addressed to, or changes sent from, anywhere else (@sec-architecture), so whatever reaches it is already on that machine. That protects the watchlist only as well as the machine's own accounts do. Any user or process on it can read the watchlist, fetch every enrolled photo and sighting crop, enrol people and purge them, and nothing records who did. A real deployment would need authentication, authorisation per operator and an audit log of every enrollment, removal, purge and model switch (#12). The SSH tunnel that gives a remote browser a `localhost` origin (@sec-reproducing) is a way to use Ryuk without them, not a substitute for them.
